passage: The economics tutorial had four minutes left, and the ceiling fan rattled so loudly that Professor Iyer had to shout. "Any questions before Friday's quiz?" Sangeeta's hand went up. "This is probably really simple, but what does marginal cost actually mean? I keep writing it without getting it." Two boys behind her snickered. Professor Iyer did not. She sketched three quick boxes on the board, one extra cup of chai, one extra rupee of cost, and ran out of time mid-sentence. Sangeeta followed her into the corridor to hear the rest. Gurleen had nodded through all of it, pen moving, face calm. On Friday, Sangeeta's answer to the second question was four lines long and right. Gurleen stared at the same question, then wrote a long paragraph that circled the term without ever landing on it.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta ask Professor Iyer?
qa.a: She asked what marginal cost actually means, because she kept writing it without getting it.

qa.q: How can you tell Sangeeta was not ashamed of her simple question?
qa.a: She raised her hand in front of everyone, called it simple without apologising, and followed the professor into the corridor; she seemed more eager to understand than embarrassed by the snickering.

qa.q: What small step could Gurleen try before the next quiz?
qa.a: Gurleen could note the one term that still feels blurry and ask the professor or Sangeeta about it, even for two minutes after class.

qa.q: How might Professor Iyer see Sangeeta's question?
qa.a: The professor probably welcomed it, since it gave a chance to explain the idea for the whole room and showed who was really trying to learn.

grounding: Shows a student who openly asks a simple question in class understanding faster than a classmate who stays quiet about being confused.

passage: Above a sweet shop in Jayanagar, the Saturday Japanese class smelled of cardamom and whiteboard markers. Sensei had just written two sentences that looked almost identical. "Any doubts?" Twelve heads nodded. Thomas nodded hardest. Anand put a hand up. "Sorry, I'm lost. Why is it 'wa' in the first one and 'ga' in the second? They both look like 'is' to me." Sensei smiled and spent ten minutes on it, with a drawing of a cat on a mat. Anand asked twice more until it clicked. Three weeks later came the speaking test. Anand described his morning in slow, uneven, correct sentences. Thomas, who had copied every note perfectly, froze after the first line and quietly said, "I understood it in class, I think."

qa.q: Where did the Saturday Japanese class meet?
qa.a: It met above a sweet shop in Jayanagar.

qa.q: What might Thomas have been worried about when he nodded hardest?
qa.a: Thomas was probably anxious about looking slow in front of eleven other people, so he pretended to understand rather than risk feeling embarrassed.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas before the next test?
qa.a: Ask one honest question per class, even a tiny one like Anand's, and practise saying sentences aloud instead of only copying notes.

qa.q: How might the other students have been affected by Anand's question?
qa.a: Some of them were probably confused too, so the cat-on-a-mat drawing helped them without their having to ask.

grounding: Shows that a learner who admits confusion in class learns faster than one who nods along and keeps the gap hidden.

passage:
"You actually asked what a standard deviation is. In third year," Gautam said, dropping his tray on the hostel mess table.
"I did," said Farida, tearing her roti. "I've been faking it since first year."
"Everyone was looking at you."
"For five seconds. Then Ma'am explained it with our cricket scores and I finally got it."
Gautam stirred his dal for a while. "Okay. Explain the cricket thing."
Farida raised an eyebrow. "You didn't get it either?"
"I nodded," he said. "I nod a lot."
"Right. If everyone in the team scores around thirty, the spread is small. If one guy scores ninety and the rest score two, it's huge. That's all it is. How far people usually are from the average."
Gautam went quiet, then laughed. "That's it? I've been memorising a formula for three years."
"Next class, you ask the next dumb question," Farida said. "I'll nod." 🙂

qa.q: How did the teacher explain standard deviation?
qa.a: Ma'am explained it with their cricket scores.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he admitted he nods a lot?
qa.a: He seemed a little embarrassed and relieved at once, since he had been memorising a formula for three years without understanding it.

qa.q: How does Farida see asking a question in front of everyone?
qa.a: To Farida it costs only five seconds of people looking, which is a small price for finally understanding something she had faked for years.

passage: "Sit, Vasudha, the tea will go cold," said Harish uncle, pushing a plate of biscuits across. "You asked how to handle that teammate who keeps saying she's useless. Let me tell you about Prakash. When I was new at the insurance office, Prakash would finish a report and sigh, 'Arre, I'm nothing, just a small clerk, this is probably full of mistakes.' Then he'd stand there. Waiting. The first month, I rushed to tell him it was brilliant. By the third month I noticed he only said it when the manager was near, and only about his best work. I felt a bit foolish for falling for it, and a bit sorry for him. One day I just said, 'Looks solid, Prakash,' and went back to my desk. He looked lost. Later he started asking me to check his numbers for real, and those were our best conversations."

qa.a: He would sigh, 'Arre, I'm nothing, just a small clerk, this is probably full of mistakes,' and then stand there waiting.

passage:
"My kaleidoscope! Who did this?" Ankita held up the cracked tube, bits of coloured glass on the floor.
Silence. Then a small shuffle under the bed.
"Nazia. Come out right now."
"No."
"You broke it on purpose because I didn't let you play!"
"I didn't!" Nazia's voice wobbled. "I was just looking. It fell. I thought you'd hate me forever."
Ankita crouched. Her little sister's face was red and wet, and her hands were shaking.
"You hid because you were scared?"
A nod.
Ankita breathed out. "I don't hate you. I'm just really, really cross."
"Can we fix it?"
"Maybe with tape." Ankita picked up a blue piece, and her jaw tightened again. "But you're not touching my things for a week."
"Okay," whispered Nazia, crawling out slowly.

qa.q: Where was Nazia hiding?
qa.a: She was under the bed.

qa.q: What did Ankita realise when she saw Nazia's face, and how did she still feel?
qa.a: She realised Nazia had hidden because she was scared, not mean, but she still felt really cross, and the anger came back when she picked up the broken glass.

qa.q: What small step could help the sisters after this?
qa.a: They could fix the kaleidoscope together with tape, so Nazia can make up for it and Ankita can calm down while doing something useful.

qa.q: How did Nazia see what happened?
qa.a: To Nazia it was an accident while looking, and she was so frightened of losing her sister's love that she hid instead of saying sorry.

passage:
Mum shouted "Amandeep, dinner!" at the exact moment I found my remote car behind the sofa with one wheel snapped off. I knew who did it. Pooja, my little sister, had been driving it into walls all afternoon.
I stomped into the kitchen ready to yell. Pooja was sitting very still, not eating, looking at her plate. When she saw the car in my hand, she started crying before I said anything.
I wanted to be angry. I was angry. But she looked like I look when I break something of Mum's and wait for trouble.
So I just said, "It was an accident, na?" She nodded so fast.
I'd like to say I stayed nice. I didn't. At bedtime the wheel still wouldn't click in, and I told her she ruined everything.

qa.a: One wheel was snapped off.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling on seeing Pooja at the table?
qa.a: Amandeep was angry but also recognised Pooja's fear, because she looked the way Amandeep looks when waiting for trouble, so the anger softened for a while.

qa.a: Amandeep could take a few breaths, put the car down for the night and say 'I'm still upset, let's try fixing it tomorrow' instead of blaming Pooja.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pooja at dinner?
qa.a: Pooja was probably scared and guilty, sitting still and not eating while she waited to be shouted at.

grounding: Shows a child realising a sibling who broke a toy was scared rather than mean, and how hard that understanding is to hold onto.

passage:
After-school centre, Thursday note.
Jatin (11) came in from the craft room holding his clay temple, one tower crushed. He went straight to Sahil, his younger brother, and grabbed his sleeve. "You sat on it!" Sahil did not argue. He stood rigid, eyes on the floor, then whispered, "Please don't tell Mummy."
Jatin let go. He asked, quite quietly, "Why are you so scared?" Sahil said Mummy had told him to be careful near Jatin's projects. Jatin looked at the crushed tower for a long time and said, "It's okay, it was clay."
Ten minutes later, when another child laughed at the temple, Jatin snapped at Sahil again.
I sat with both boys, helped them reshape the tower together, and mentioned the good moment to their mother at pickup.

qa.q: What did Sahil whisper when Jatin grabbed his sleeve?
qa.a: He whispered, 'Please don't tell Mummy.'

qa.q: What changed in Jatin when he asked Sahil why he was so scared?
qa.a: Jatin's anger eased into understanding; he seemed to feel sorry for Sahil once he saw his brother was frightened, not careless on purpose.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next, and why did it help?
qa.a: They sat with both boys and helped them reshape the tower together, which let Jatin cool down and let Sahil make amends.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the moment when Jatin said it was only clay?
qa.a: Sahil was probably hugely relieved, since he had been expecting trouble and his brother chose kindness instead.

grounding: Shows a child briefly understanding that his brother broke his model out of fear, not meanness, before anger returns.

passage: The hostel phone booth at Sunbeam Residential School had a queue, and Zainab didn't care who heard. "Abbu, everyone is going on the trek! It's two days! You never let me do anything!" passage:
Amma,

I'm writing this because every time I try to say it out loud, we both start shouting again.

Last night, when you took my phone after I came home at eleven from Zainab's birthday, I thought you were the most unfair person alive. I said things I shouldn't have. In that moment all I could see was how embarrassed I felt in front of Zainab's mother, and how you "never trust me."

This morning, lying awake, I remembered you standing at the gate in your nightie. You'd called me seven times. My phone was on silent. I think you were scared something had happened to me.

I'm still a bit annoyed about the phone. But I get it now, more than I did at eleven o'clock.

Your daughter,
Ganga

qa.q: What time did Ganga come home from Zainab's birthday?
qa.a: Ganga came home at eleven.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling during the quarrel the night before?
qa.a: Ganga felt angry and embarrassed in front of Zainab's mother, and convinced that Amma was being unfair and did not trust her.

"Avni, don't laugh, okay? Last night I had the biggest fight with Papa. Like, door-slamming level.

passage: The power went at eight, right in the middle of exam week. Vijay sat on the stairs with the phone torch, his mock-test paper crumpled in his fist. Thirty-one out of a hundred. "My life is finished," he muttered. Sharmila, his older sister, rolled her eyes, but Dadi called them both to the veranda where the candle was burning. She didn't give advice. She told them about the year she was fifteen, when her father's shop burned down and she had to leave school for two years to help. "I cried every night. Then I went back, finished, became a teacher. Thirty-eight years I taught." She laughed softly. "The fire felt like the end. It was one bad chapter." Vijay smoothed the paper on his knee. The power came back an hour later, but he stayed on the veranda.

qa.a: Thirty-one out of a hundred.

qa.q: How can you tell Dadi's story changed how Vijay felt?

qa.q: What small step could help Vijay after the veranda talk?
qa.a: He could look at which questions he got wrong with his teacher or Sharmila and plan the next week's revision, treating the test as one chapter.

qa.a: Her own years of loss and return let Vijay feel a longer timeline himself, which a lecture about marks probably could not have done.

grounding: Shows a grandmother's story of hardship giving a teenager a longer view of his own setback, more than advice could.

passage:
Two hundred people, a microphone, and my mind went completely white.
I was presenting our club's water-filter idea at the college innovation summit. I got as far as "Good morning, esteemed judges" and then nothing. Twenty seconds of nothing. Someone coughed. I read the rest off my phone like a robot.
Afterwards I sat on the steps behind the auditorium and wanted to disappear. Wasim sat down next to me with two samosas.
"Raghav," he said, "in a year, who's going to talk about this?"
I thought about it properly. The judges had seen forty teams. My club mates were already arguing about lunch. My parents would hear the funny version.
"Honestly? Me," I said.
It still burned. It still burns a bit now. But on those steps, it became one bad morning instead of my whole reputation.

qa.q: How long did Raghav's mind stay blank?
qa.a: Twenty seconds of nothing.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel sitting on the steps behind the auditorium?
qa.a: Raghav felt humiliated and wanted to disappear after blanking in front of two hundred people.

qa.q: What small step could Raghav take before the next presentation?
qa.a: Raghav could practise the opening lines aloud in front of a couple of friends so the first minute feels automatic under pressure.

qa.q: How does Wasim seem to see the disaster?
qa.a: Wasim seems to see it as a painful but passing moment, bringing samosas and asking the one-year question instead of dismissing Raghav's feelings.

grounding: Shows a young adult zooming out in time and to other people after freezing on stage, which cuts the drama without denying the sting.

Dear Disha,

I've coached debate for eleven years, and you are the sharpest speaker I've had. When you took apart the other team's economic case in the finals, the judges stopped writing.

That is why I'm writing. This year you won every argument and, I think, lost a few things that mattered more. You argued your way out of the lab project and left Rhea to finish it alone. You told me the scholarship interview was "beneath" you because they asked a lazy question. You haven't come to practice since the finals, and I miss you there.

Being clever tells you how to win a point. It doesn't tell you which points are worth winning.

My door is open on Tuesdays, if you want to talk it through.

Lokesh

passage:
"You want to hear about the one who taught me the most? I'm Damini, and I've been a maths tutor in Bhopal for nine years. His name was Vikas.
He was nineteen and faster than me. Genuinely. He'd find the flaw in any proof I put on the board, and he'd argue with his parents the same way. He argued his way out of engineering, then out of the design course, then out of the job his uncle offered. Every time, he had a perfect case.
Last winter I met him at the bus stand. He was working nights at a call centre, tired, still arguing, this time with the bus conductor about change.
I used to think if you're clever enough, life sorts itself. Vikas taught me that being able to win every debate is not the same as knowing what's worth fighting for."

qa.q: Where did Damini meet Vikas last winter?
qa.a: At the bus stand.

qa.q: What does Damini seem to feel on recalling the meeting with Vikas at the bus stand?
qa.a: Damini seems saddened and a little regretful, seeing that the brilliant student who could win every argument ended up tired and stuck.

qa.q: What could a tutor like Damini try with a student like Vikas?
qa.a: Instead of only admiring the arguments, the tutor could ask questions like 'What do you want in five years, and does this choice help?'

qa.q: What might Vikas's parents have experienced during his teenage years?
qa.a: They probably felt frustrated and worn out, losing every argument while watching him drop course after course.

grounding: Shows a tutor observing a brilliant student who wins every argument yet keeps making poor life choices.

passage:
I run the physics lab in the second-year block, so I see everyone. Tushar stands out. When Professor Sen made an error in a derivation, Tushar caught it and defended his correction for twenty minutes until the professor gave up. The class clapped.
But I also see the attendance register. He's missed half the practicals this term because he "already knows the results." Last week he argued with the canteen staff that his late fee was illegal and won, then missed the viva.
I don't know what's going on inside him. Maybe he's bored. Maybe something at home. He always has an answer when I ask, and it's always a clever one.
Yesterday he left his lab file on the bench. It was empty after page three. I kept it, and I'll hand it back tomorrow and ask how I can help.

qa.q: How many practicals has Tushar missed this term?
qa.a: He has missed half the practicals this term.

qa.q: What does the narrator seem to feel about Tushar, and why?
qa.a: The observer is uncertain what is going on inside Tushar, wondering whether he is bored or something at home is troubling him, and is concerned for him.

qa.q: What small step does the observer plan, and why could it help?
qa.a: Handing back the file and asking how they can help opens a real conversation about his choices instead of another argument.

qa.q: How might Professor Sen see Tushar?
qa.a: The professor probably sees a gifted but exhausting student, impressive at spotting errors but hard to guide toward what actually matters.

grounding: Shows an observer in a lab noticing a clever student who wins arguments yet neglects the work that counts.

passage: In the hospital canteen at St. Anne's, Nandini had a notebook open next to her idli. The offer from the cancer centre in Hyderabad was for night-shift ICU. It was the work she had trained for, but it was four hundred kilometres from her mother. Over three days she asked people. Sister Vasudha, who had moved cities at twenty-four, said, "The first year is lonely. Then you make a family there." Leela from pharmacy said never do nights, they wreck you. Her old tutor said go, you're wasting yourself here. Nandini wrote each answer down, then wrote a second column: what I care about. Learning. Being reachable for Amma. She stared at it until her tea went cold. Then she called Hyderabad to ask one more question: could she switch to days after a year?

qa.q: How far was the Hyderabad centre from Nandini's mother?
qa.a: It was four hundred kilometres from her mother.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling as she stared at her two columns?
qa.a: Nandini felt torn between the learning she wanted and her worry about being far from Amma.

qa.q: Which part of Nandini's approach worked well?
qa.a: She asked several people who had lived through similar moves, then weighed their answers against her own list of what she cares about instead of just obeying one voice.

qa.q: How might Sister Vasudha see Nandini's decision?
qa.a: Having moved cities herself, Sister Vasudha probably understands the loneliness ahead and would respect whichever choice Nandini makes for her own reasons.

grounding: Shows a young adult consulting people who had faced similar moves and weighing their views against her own values before deciding.

passage:
Subject: The thing I've been going back and forth about

Hi Sahil,

You asked what I decided about the master's in Leeds. Here's where I am.

I talked to four people. Your cousin, who went abroad and came back, said it changed how she thinks. My old manager said skills matter more than the degree. Kavitha aunty, who did hers at thirty, said don't rush. And Papa said, quietly, that he'd be fine alone, which is exactly what someone says when they won't be.

Everyone was right about their own life. None of them were living mine.

So I wrote down what I care about: learning, being near Papa while his knee heals, not waiting forever. I've deferred by one year. It's my call, and I feel strangely calm about it.

Talk soon,
Jaya

qa.q: How many people did Jaya talk to about the master's?
qa.a: She talked to four people.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel after making the decision?
qa.a: Jaya felt strangely calm, because the choice came from her own list of what she cares about.

qa.q: What would you advise someone facing a choice like Jaya's?
qa.a: Ask a few people who have lived through something similar, then list your own values and decide from that list, as Jaya did.

qa.q: What might Papa have been feeling when he said he'd be fine alone?
qa.a: He was probably trying to protect Jaya's plans while quietly worrying about coping alone with his knee.

grounding: Shows a young adult who asked widely among people with similar experience and still made the final decision from Jaya's own values.

passage:
"You want the honest version, Sudha? I'm Darshan, twenty-five, and six months ago I was writing code for a bank and dreaming about teaching.
I didn't just jump. I asked people. My school physics teacher said teaching is joy and exhaustion in equal parts. A college friend who left software to teach said the first year nearly broke her. My uncle said I was throwing everything away. A stranger at a workshop told me she'd never been happier.
All of them were telling me the truth about their own lives. So I sat down one Sunday with a notebook. What makes my day feel worth it? Explaining things. Watching someone get it. Code gave me neither.
So I chose it, knowing the exhaustion part was real. My uncle still grumbles. But it was my choice, and I'd make it again."

qa.q: What did Darshan's school physics teacher say about teaching?
qa.a: The teacher said teaching is joy and exhaustion in equal parts.

qa.q: What does Darshan's Sunday notebook show about how Darshan was feeling?
qa.a: It shows Darshan was unsure and a bit torn after hearing so many different views, and wanted to settle it by checking what truly made his day feel worth it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Darshan's decision, and why did it work?
qa.a: Writing down what made the day feel worthwhile turned many opinions into one clear value, so the choice was Darshan's own and not just the loudest advice.

qa.q: How might Darshan's uncle see the career change?
qa.a: The uncle probably sees it as a risky waste of a secure job and is still worried, even though Darshan made the choice with care.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking several people with similar experience and then weighing their views against their own values to decide.

passage: At the park in Dublin, Liam was filling his yellow digger with sand. A little girl, Nour, stood close, watching. "Liam, let Nour have a turn," said Mum. Liam held the digger tight. "Mine." "Just a short turn, love. Sharing is kind." Slowly, Liam opened his hands. Nour grabbed it and ran to the slide. Liam's lip wobbled. He sat very still in the sand, staring after his digger, fists pressed into his knees. Mum knelt and rubbed his back. "That was hard, wasn't it?" He nodded and leaned into her.

qa.q: What colour was Liam's digger?
qa.a: It was yellow.

qa.q: How can you tell Liam felt sad after giving Nour the digger?
qa.a: His lip wobbled, he sat very still staring after it with his fists pressed into his knees, and he leaned into Mum.

qa.q: What did Mum do well after Liam shared?
qa.a: She knelt, rubbed his back and named that it was hard, so Liam's feeling of loss was noticed and not brushed aside.

qa.q: What would change if Liam had chosen to share on his own?
qa.a: He might have felt proud instead of only losing something, and the sharing would have been his own gift rather than an instruction.

grounding: Shows a young child handing over a toy after a parent urges it and feeling the loss sharply.

passage: The clinic waiting room was full. Zubin, five, zoomed his little red car along the bench. Beside them, a boy named Arnab was crying and pointing at the car. "Zubin, beta, give it to him for a bit," Papa said. "He's poorly." Zubin looked at Papa, then at the car. Papa nodded again. Zubin held it out without looking. Arnab stopped crying at once. Zubin climbed into Papa's lap, pressed his face against Papa's shirt, and stayed there, very quiet, peeking at his car every few seconds.

qa.q: Where were Zubin and Papa waiting?
qa.a: In the clinic waiting room.

qa.q: What does Zubin peeking at his car every few seconds suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Zubin still missed his car and felt a little sad, even though he had handed it over.

qa.q: How could Papa support Zubin after this?
qa.a: Papa could hug him and say, 'That was hard, and it helped Arnab,' and make sure the car comes back before they leave.

qa.q: How might Arnab's family see Zubin's action?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and grateful that the crying stopped in a crowded waiting room.

grounding: Shows a young child giving up a toy at a parent's urging while clearly feeling the loss.

passage:
Monday: Cousin Raghav came to visit. Mama said, "Kamal, share your spinning top." Kamal handed it over and then cried in the corner till Raghav left.
Wednesday: Raghav came again. Kamal hid the top under his pillow before the doorbell stopped ringing.
Saturday: Kamal watched Papa hold his big umbrella over the neighbour at the gate. Later, when Raghav visited, Kamal took out the top. He held it for a long moment. Then he gave it to Raghav, all by himself. He watched it spin, a little worried, and clapped when it wobbled back.

qa.q: Where did Kamal hide the top on Wednesday?
qa.a: Under his pillow.

qa.q: How was Kamal feeling on Saturday when he held the top for a long moment?
qa.a: He felt a little worried and unsure about letting go, but chose to share it anyway.

qa.q: What could Mama try next time instead of telling Kamal to share?
qa.a: She could let Kamal decide, maybe asking, 'Would you like to give Raghav a turn?' and praising him when he chooses to.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Saturday for Raghav?
qa.a: On Monday Raghav got the top from an order and Kamal cried; on Saturday he got it as a gift and Kamal clapped with him.

grounding: Shows a child moving from forced sharing, felt as loss, to sharing on his own after copying his father's kindness.

passage: It was drizzling in Lisbon, and Beatriz's lunch had fallen into a puddle on the way to school. At break she sat on the bench with nothing, arms crossed, pretending not to care. Mina noticed. Nobody told her to do anything. She opened her box, looked at her cheese sandwich, and tore it carefully down the middle. "Here. The bigger half's yours, I had a big breakfast." Beatriz blinked, then smiled and took it. They ate together under the covered walkway, crumbs everywhere. Walking back to class, Mina felt a warm, fizzy feeling in her chest. At home that evening she told her mother, "I think I'm a sharing sort of person." Her mother laughed and asked why. Mina told her the whole story, twice.

qa.q: What happened to Beatriz's lunch?
qa.a: It had fallen into a puddle on the way to school.

qa.q: What was Mina feeling as she walked back to class?
qa.a: She felt warm and happy, a fizzy feeling in her chest after sharing her sandwich.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering the bigger half with a light excuse worked, because Beatriz could accept the food without feeling embarrassed.

qa.q: How might Beatriz have felt before Mina came over?
qa.a: Beatriz was probably hungry and embarrassed, crossing her arms and pretending not to care.

grounding: Shows a child freely sharing lunch with a classmate who has none, feeling warm afterwards and starting to see herself as generous.

passage: Pallavi saw Nazia open her empty bag at lunch break in Class 5B and go pink. "Forgot my tiffin. Mummy left early for the hospital shift." Around them, the classroom filled with smells of dal and parathas. Nobody had said a word to Pallavi, but she pushed her steel box across. "Take two parathas. I've got four, I can't finish." Nazia hesitated, then took them. "Thank you." "With the pickle, it's better," Pallavi said. The rest of the day, Pallavi kept smiling at nothing. When the teacher asked the class to write one good thing they did this week, she wrote about the parathas without even thinking.

qa.q: Why did Nazia forget her tiffin?
qa.a: Her Mummy left early for the hospital shift.

qa.q: How can you tell Pallavi felt good after sharing?
qa.a: She kept smiling at nothing for the rest of the day and chose the parathas as her good deed without even thinking, which shows she felt proud and warm.

qa.q: What small step helped Nazia accept the food easily?
qa.a: Pallavi said she had four and couldn't finish, and offered the pickle too, which made taking the food feel ordinary rather than like charity.

qa.q: What was it like for Nazia when she opened her empty bag?
qa.a: She went pink, so she was probably embarrassed and worried about going hungry in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a child freely sharing half her lunch with a classmate without being asked, and feeling warm about it afterwards.

passage:
Tuesday: Binita noticed Bidisha sitting on the steps at lunch, not eating. "My mother's got the new baby, she forgot to pack," Bidisha said, shrugging. Binita ate her luchi fast and felt oddly bad about it.
Wednesday: Same steps. This time Binita sat down and split her tiffin before she could think. "Half-half." Bidisha grinned. Binita felt warm all through maths.
The next Monday: Binita asked her Ma, all by herself, to pack a little extra "just in case." Ma raised an eyebrow. "For who?" "For whoever needs it. I'm good at sharing now," Binita said, and Ma smiled.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha have no lunch on Tuesday?
qa.a: Her mother had the new baby and forgot to pack.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on Tuesday after eating fast?
qa.a: She felt oddly bad, a small guilty pang at eating while Bidisha had nothing.

qa.q: What would you advise Binita if Bidisha keeps coming without lunch?
qa.a: Keep sharing kindly, and also mention it to Ma or the class teacher so an adult can check the family is managing with the new baby.

qa.q: How might Ma see Binita's request for extra food?
qa.a: Ma is surprised at first but seems pleased and proud that Binita thought of it on her own.

grounding: Shows a child moving from noticing a hungry classmate to freely sharing and then seeing herself as someone who gives.
